cards.explanation: The city is Rome. Paul says, "I must see Rome as well." (Acts 19:21) He says it after he has been to Jerusalem. The man hasn't even left for Jerusalem yet and he's already penciling in the next city. I can't plan past tomorrow's batch, so I'm impressed.

Paul stays behind for a time. Timothy and Erastus go ahead to Macedonia, while Paul "…stayed for a time in the province of Asia." (Acts 19:22) Timothy is one of Paul's helpers, and so is Erastus. Paul sends them off, and he stays put for a time.

The word is business. The silver shrines of Artemis bring "…much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Demetrius is the silversmith who makes them. The text says much business, friends, not a little.

The man is Paul, the apostle. Demetrius says, "…this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away." (Acts 19:26) Notice he says it to the craftsmen, who make their living from those shrines. He's got their full attention.

The answer is True. Demetrius says of Paul, "He says that man-made gods are no gods at all." (Acts 19:26) That's Demetrius describing Paul's message to the craftsmen and the workmen in related trades he gathered (Acts 19:25). I bet that message did not go over well with people whose business was shrines.

The answer is True. Demetrius warns that "…the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed…" (Acts 19:27) So he's worried about more than his own paycheck. He brings the temple into it too.

They start shouting. "When the men heard this, they were enraged and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:28) Demetrius finished talking, and the volume went straight up. Their first move after hearing him is to shout.

The two men are Gaius and Aristarchus. The crowd rushed into the theatre, "…dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s traveling companions from Macedonia." (Acts 19:29) Imagine just trying to travel with a friend and getting pulled into this.

The answer is False. The text says, "Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him." (Acts 19:30) So the disciples did not let him go before the assembly. I think that was a good friend move.

These friends are officials of the province of Asia. "Even some of Paul’s friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre." (Acts 19:31) They didn't just ask, friends, they begged. These are friends of Paul who hold office in the province.

The answer is False. "Some were shouting one thing and some another, and most of them did not even know why they were there." (Acts 19:32) That says most of them, not every last person. A lot of people shouting, and most of them not knowing why.

The first thing Alexander does is motion for silence. He "…motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people." (Acts 19:33) He's the man the Jews in the crowd pushed forward. He gets his hand up first and plans to talk next.

They all shout over him together. Alexander motions for silence so he can make his defense (Acts 19:33). Then "…when they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:34) The verse records two hours of the same shout.

The answer is True. After the city clerk quieted the crowd, he declared, "…doesn’t everyone know that the city of Ephesus is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven?" (Acts 19:35) He's reminding them of something he says everyone knows. The quieting comes first, and then he speaks.

The answer is False. The clerk says the men "…have neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess." (Acts 19:37) So he says they have not blasphemed her. That's a clear statement from the city clerk, in front of the whole crowd.

The clerk points them to the courts. He says, "…the courts are open and proconsuls are available. Let them bring charges against one another there." (Acts 19:38) A proconsul is a Roman governor. That's where he sends Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen if they have a complaint.
The word is legal. The clerk says, "…it must be settled in a legal assembly." (Acts 19:39) A proper meeting with proper rules, friends, not a theatre full of people shouting different things.

The word is rioting. The clerk says, "…we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events…" (Acts 19:40) He says "we," so he counts himself in. I think he's telling them to calm down before it gets worse.

He dismisses the assembly. "After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41) First the clerk quieted the crowd (Acts 19:35). Then he spoke, and then he dismissed them. Before that, they had shouted for about two hours (Acts 19:34).
